transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-29
Start: 09:15 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen; Priya Nair; Marco Ruiz; Rachel Park; Ethan Morales; Sandra Kim; Devon Lee
Recording ID: ff-20251229-0215-canary-001

Summary:
Quick weekly sync for week 6 of the Private pilot. Focus was on the canary upgrade to kernel v1.14, two unexpected fallback events during the last 48h, and remaining telemetry gaps for long-tail latency analysis. Decided on artefact sharing and next steps for a runbook walkthrough.

Topics:
- Canary kernel v1.14 rollout results and observed latency regressions
- Fallback routing behavior (policy, partial vs full fallback)
- VPC egress/DNS flapping incidents and BGP/route reflections
- KV cache performance under quantized model profile
- Telemetry/observability: missing span context across proxy hops

Action items (recapped in call): see action_items field

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam Chen: Alright everyone thanks for joining, um let's do a quick 60 second status — I'm gonna hand to Priya to summarize the canary metrics and then Marco will cover the network flaps.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Cool, thanks Liam. So in canary week 6 we rolled kernel v1.14 to 3 of 12 nodes in the dedicated pool at 02:00 UTC last night. Baseline latency looked good for small seqs but we saw a tail increase at around 30 to 120 ms for mid-size seqs, like 512 to 1k tokens, which is odd because optimization path should've improved ATT (attention) perf. Some transcriptions show the metric as A-T-T but it's attention. There were two fallback triggers — one at 03:22 and one at 06:07 UTC.
[00:45] Rachel Park: Can you be a bit more specific about 'fallback trigger'? Was that automatic per policy or a manual intervention?
[00:52] Priya Nair: Automatic — the canary reached threshold on 95th percentile latency exceeding the SLO for three consecutive minutes, so the smart router moved a subset of traffic to the pre-quantized variant and then to the regional fallback. There was some jitter though — the routing policy didn't fully drain KV cache, so we saw cache misses in the fallback path.
[01:20] Ethan Morales: Wait, so when it moved to fallback it didn't warm the KV cache? I thought the router preserves prefixes and kv-refs?
[01:28] Priya Nair: Yeah that's the intent, but there's an edge case — the policy does prefix-hinting, but because the request hash changed slightly due to a header rewrite at our ingress proxy, the cache key didn't hit. Basically small header normalization caused cache miss and then cold-start latency.
[01:45] Marco Ruiz: To add, on the network side we saw some VPC egress route churn in the customer transit gateway at 06:05 UTC which coincided with the second fallback. There looks like there was a short-lived DNS flap — some names resolved to the wrong AZ so the internal load balancer sent traffic to a node that didn't have the latest model shard.
[02:10] Devon Lee: I ran an initial traceroute and saw a pair of AS path changes, it looked like the cloud provider did a micro BGP reconvergence, but timing is fuzzy. We'll attach the traceroutes.
[02:25] Sandra Kim: From security side: the KMS policy was untouched, rotation windows are the same. We do need a clearer articulation of the key usage in private mode though — are we sending plaintext to Redwood logs? we asked earlier but wasn't fully answered.
[02:44] Liam Chen: Good point. Redwood doesn't ingest customer plaintext; keys remain customer-managed by default in the private flow, and any artifacts we request will be scrubbed. We'll provide the KMS policy snapshot.
[02:58] Priya Nair: Back to the canary perf — we instrumented per-route token breakdowns. Most of the tail came from the 600-900 token range with batch sizes of 8-12. When the cache missed we saw multiplier effect: cold KV fetch + kernel scheduling jitter + egress retry.
[03:22] Rachel Park: Do you think it's a bug in the kernel v1.14 scheduler or an interaction with our ingress?
[03:28] Priya Nair: Early data suggests interaction. We saw one spike where CPU steal went up on the host (that's Luigi again, remind me to check the host box name), and that correlated with an ingress garbage collector cycle on the customer's side. So higher host contention plus cache miss = tail. We're not ruling out a kernel scheduling change, but so far the correlation points to multi-factor.
[03:50] Marco Ruiz: The BPF traces we pulled show a couple of unusual syscalls around socket connect/reuse that line up with the egress flaps. We'll export them.
[04:06] Ethan Morales: Do you have an ETA on the full log pack? The pcap you mentioned earlier?
[04:10] Priya Nair: Yes, I'll assemble trimmed logs and pcaps and share to the secure bucket. We'll redact PII.
[04:18] Devon Lee: Also worth noting, our internal canary traffic rate was a bit higher than expected because our test harness ramped up faster — that might've amplified the edge case.
[04:30] Liam Chen: Ok, let's talk fallback policy — currently it's a two-step: variant fallback then regional fallback. Is there appetite to add an intermediate degraded mode that keeps cache keys stable?
[04:44] Rachel Park: Yes if we can keep cache warm that'd reduce tail. But any solution needs to be safe for us from a data residency perspective — can't spill cross-region keys.
[04:55] Priya Nair: We can implement sticky-prefix routing for a short window — hold traffic bound to same KV shard for X minutes during failover. That requires a small router policy change and a canary to validate.
[05:08] Sandra Kim: That sounds OK but we need to see the policy JSON and the cryptographic assumptions — does it increase attack surface?
[05:18] Marco Ruiz: It doesn't change encryption at rest or KMS scope, just the routing sticky key. We'll provide a threat model note.
[05:26] Liam Chen: On telemetry: we saw missing span context on a few hops — trace IDs dropped at the edge proxy so we couldn't join traces across the router. That's a gap we need to close to root cause the long tail.
[05:40] Priya Nair: Action: we'll push a small header-preserve fix in the ingress shim used for the pilot and re-run the microbench.
[05:49] Ethan Morales: For the KV cache microbench, do you have the script we should execute?
[05:53] Priya Nair: Yes, it's in the pilot repo — I'll share the path and a runbook snippet. There's a corner case with randomized prefixes, so set seed=42.
[06:02] Rachel Park: Can we also increase observability retention for one week so we can inspect the 95/99th windows?
[06:08] Liam Chen: Redwood can enable a 14-day retention on telemetry for this pilot as part of support package; I'll follow up with billing to avoid surprises.
[06:20] Sandra Kim: Also, on compliance: SOC2 artifacts — do you have the SOC2 Type II report we requested?
[06:26] Liam Chen: Yes we provided the security pack earlier, but I'll re-send the cert and the SOC2 link directly to Sandra and legal.
[06:33] Devon Lee: Quick question: when fallback happened, were function/tool calls preserved, or did the model responses change schema? We have downstream parsing that is schema-sensitive.
[06:43] Priya Nair: The fallback maintained the same response schema; there were some tokenization differences because pre-quantized model variant uses a slightly different tokenizer version. We can pin tokenizer model and force exact token mapping in the fallback path if needed.
[06:58] Rachel Park: That might be important for our NLU parser. If tokenization changes, downstream parsing confidence drops.
[07:06] Priya Nair: Agreed — we'll include a pinned tokenizer option in the routing policy.
[07:14] Marco Ruiz: About the BGP reconverge note: our hypothesis — provider side route flap led to transient node shadowing, LB picked the node without latest shard, that triggered cache coldness and then router fallback.
[07:28] Ethan Morales: Any way to make the router more conservative and only fallback when cache hit ratio < X AND latency > Y?
[07:36] Priya Nair: Yes that's feasible — combine metrics. We'll demo a policy that gates fallback on hit ratio < 0.7 and 95th > threshold. That reduces false positives.
[07:48] Rachel Park: Please include an override channel for manual rollback. We had an incident where automatic fallback looped and caused extra churn.
[07:55] Liam Chen: Manual override is in the console — we can add an extra guard with a 5-minute cooldown.
[08:03] Sandra Kim: On the KMS question again — when you request logs, please provide a hash-only index rather than full request payloads.
[08:12] Priya Nair: We'll provide redacted logs and a hash index; if you want we can provide a differential pack showing only the changed fields.
[08:20] Devon Lee: Are there any other service dependencies you observed? Any third-party CDN or WAF involvement?
[08:26] Marco Ruiz: Not directly in our traces; the only extra hop was the customer's regional proxy.
[08:30] Liam Chen: Ok let's summarize the decisions: 1) collect and share logs/pcaps 2) implement sticky-prefix short window as intermediate fallback 3) preserve trace headers and rerun microbench 4) provide policy JSON and threat model 5) extend telemetry retention temporarily
[08:52] Rachel Park: That reads right. For scheduling the runbook walkthrough, can we do Jan 7 or Jan 8 US times?
[08:58] Liam Chen: Jan 7 10am PT works for Redwood — I'll send invite.
[09:04] Priya Nair: I'll also attach the run commands and the seed for the KV microbench; please post results to the secure bucket.
[09:12] Ethan Morales: One edge note — our legal asked about cross-region fallback log retention for GDPR; Sandra will confirm what data we can share.
[09:20] Sandra Kim: We'll redact any EU PII, should be fine.
[09:26] Liam Chen: Great, thanks everyone. Any final questions?
[09:30] Rachel Park: None from me.
[09:32] Devon Lee: No.
[09:34] Liam Chen: Alright we'll close. Post-call I'll follow up with the security pack and the policy JSON.
[09:40] (call ends)
